text: Selecting the right patent agent/attorney for AYUSH: 1) Technical background — pharma/chemistry/biotech education. 2) AYUSH experience — familiarity with Section 3(d), 3(p), TKDL. 3) Registration — registered with Indian Patent Office. 4) Track record — granted patents in similar field. 5) Communication — explains complex issues clearly. 6) Fees — transparent, competitive (Rs 30,000-80,000 for drafting/filing, Rs 15,000-40,000 for prosecution responses). 7) References — check with other AYUSH companies. Interview multiple agents before selecting.

Patent Agent: registered with Patent Office to practice before it, can draft and prosecute patents, cannot appear in courts. Patent Attorney: both patent agent AND advocate (lawyer), can handle prosecution AND litigation. Trademark Agent: registered under Trade Marks Act. For AYUSH: use patent agent for prosecution, patent attorney or IP litigation lawyer for enforcement/opposition matters. Many firms have both; ensure right specialist handles each task.

Effective IP counsel engagement: 1) Provide clear, complete technical information. 2) Explain what's novel — what you invented vs what's known. 3) Share prior art you know about. 4) Discuss business objectives — which claims matter most. 5) Review drafts carefully — you know the technology best. 6) Respond promptly to queries. 7) Budget realistically — good IP work takes time. 8) Build long-term relationship — continuity helps. For AYUSH: educate your agent about Ayurveda if they lack background; provide classical text references.

In-house IP team vs external counsel: In-house advantages: lower per-matter cost at scale, better integration with R&D, faster turnaround, institutional knowledge. External advantages: specialized expertise, scalability, no fixed cost, objectivity. Hybrid model: in-house for strategy and first review, external for drafting and prosecution. For AYUSH startups: external counsel initially; consider in-house IP manager as portfolio grows beyond 10-20 patents.

IP audit identifies and evaluates all IP assets: Process: 1) Inventory — list all patents, trademarks, copyrights, trade secrets. 2) Ownership verification — proper assignments in place? 3) Maintenance status — renewals paid, not abandoned? 4) Valuation — commercial significance. 5) Risk assessment — FTO issues, infringement exposure. 6) Recommendations — gaps, opportunities, improvements. Conduct IP audit: annually, before M&A, before major product launch. For AYUSH: audit should cover formulation IP, brand protection, and regulatory data.

Training researchers on IP: Key topics: 1) What's patentable — novelty, inventive step, exclusions. 2) Importance of confidentiality — don't publish before filing. 3) Lab notebooks — contemporaneous records supporting inventorship. 4) Invention disclosure process — when and how to report. 5) Prior art awareness — document what you find. 6) Assignment obligations — employment agreement terms. For AYUSH R&D teams: regular training sessions, clear invention disclosure forms, designated IP coordinator.

Invention disclosure form captures key information: 1) Title/description of invention. 2) Inventors — who conceived each element. 3) Problem solved. 4) Prior art known. 5) Reduction to practice status — lab scale, pilot, commercial? 6) Publications/presentations — past and planned. 7) Commercial potential. 8) Supporting data. For AYUSH: include formulation details, experimental results, comparison with existing treatments. Form triggers IP evaluation — decide patent/trade secret/publish strategy.

Lab notebooks support patent claims: Best practices: 1) Bound notebooks with numbered pages. 2) Contemporaneous entries — record when work is done. 3) Complete details — enough for reproduction. 4) Sign and date entries. 5) Have witness sign important entries (someone who understands but didn't do the work). 6) No blank spaces, crossed-out errors, or torn pages. 7) Retain permanently. Electronic notebooks: if used, ensure audit trail, backup, authentication. For AYUSH: notebooks prove conception date, inventorship, and enablement.

IP budget considerations for AYUSH: Patent filing (India): Rs 50,000-1,00,000 (drafting + official fees). Prosecution: Rs 30,000-60,000 per response. Renewal: Rs 800-40,000/year (increases over time). PCT: Rs 2-3 lakh filing + Rs 1.5-3 lakh per country national phase. Trademark: Rs 10,000-20,000 per class. Trade secret: nominal (NDAs, security systems). Total portfolio cost grows; budget 2-5% of R&D spend for IP protection. Prioritize: focus on commercially important innovations.

IP insurance options: 1) Enforcement insurance — covers litigation costs to enforce your IP. 2) Defense insurance — covers costs defending infringement claims. 3) Abatement insurance — covers business losses during disputes. 4) First-party coverage — your costs. 5) Third-party liability — damages you owe others. Availability in India: limited; global insurers offer some coverage. Consider for: valuable patents, products in competitive markets, exports to US (litigious). Premium: 1-3% of coverage.

IP docketing manages deadlines: Key deadlines: 1) Priority claim — 12 months from first filing. 2) PCT national phase — 30/31 months. 3) RFE filing — 48 months. 4) FER response — 6+3 months. 5) Renewal payments — annual. 6) Working statements — annual June 30. 7) Opposition deadlines — varies. Tools: Excel for small portfolios, IP management software (Anaqua, CPA Global, Foundation IP) for larger. Missing deadline can abandon patent — docketing is critical. For AYUSH: assign responsibility, use calendar alerts, verify with professional.

Managing IP across countries: 1) Use PCT to defer and centralize early stage. 2) Coordinate with local counsel in each country. 3) Maintain central database of all filings. 4) Standardize processes — consistent invention disclosure, evaluation. 5) Budget for multi-jurisdiction costs. 6) Prioritize markets — can't afford everywhere, focus on commercially important countries. 7) Monitor for deadlines across jurisdictions. For AYUSH exporters: India + US + EU + GCC covers most markets; add specific countries based on business plan.

IP due diligence for transactions (M&A, licensing, investment): Review areas: 1) Ownership — clean chain of title, proper assignments. 2) Validity — prior art issues, prosecution history. 3) Scope — claim coverage of target products. 4) Encumbrances — existing licenses, liens. 5) Maintenance — fees paid, not abandoned. 6) Litigation — pending disputes. 7) FTO — third-party IP risks. Red flags: missing assignments, unpaid fees, pending oppositions, broad prior art. For AYUSH: add check for NBA compliance, TKDL issues, traditional knowledge concerns.
